html:
From 1688 about two hundred French Protestant refugees, the Huguenots, settled at the Dutch colony at the Cape of Good Hope. Many were given farms in a valley that became known as Franschhoek, "French corner", where they helped build the Cape wine industry.

They had fled France after Louis XIV outlawed Protestantism in 1685 with the Edict of Fontainebleau. Tens of thousands went to the Netherlands in the Huguenot exodus, and the Dutch East India Company offered free passage and land to some, as it wanted more farmers at the Cape. A few knew how to grow grapes and make wine, which had been made at the Cape since 1659.

The company did not want a separate French community. Within two generations the Huguenots spoke Dutch and married into the other settler families. They became part of the Afrikaners, and many Afrikaner surnames, such as du Toit, Joubert, du Plessis and de Villiers, come from them.
